title: The 5 Biggest Snakes Ever Found, and Why Titanoboa Is Gone
description: A 50-foot snake from India is back in the news, a wild python just set a Guinness record, and Titanoboa still holds the crown. We count down the five biggest snakes ever measured, and end with the real reason no snake that big is alive today.

scenes.say: A real snake once grew to about thirteen meters. That's forty-two feet.

scenes.label: Back in the news
scenes.say: And this month, the news put a second monster back in the headlines. A snake from India that might have rivaled it.

scenes.label: Five giants
scenes.say: Okay, so here's the plan. We'll count down the five biggest snakes ever measured, from big, to bigger, to ridiculous.

scenes.label: Stay for the end
scenes.say: And stay to the very end. Because the last one explains why no snake that big is alive today. And the answer is not what you think.

scenes.label: Wait, how?
scenes.say: Quick thing first. How do you even measure a snake that died millions of years ago?

scenes.label: 300+ vertebrae
scenes.say: Here's the trick. Snakes are mostly backbone. A big anaconda can have more than three hundred vertebrae.

scenes.label: One bone, one estimate
scenes.say: So scientists measure one fossil vertebra, compare it to living snakes, and estimate the whole body. It's clever. But it's never perfect.

scenes.label: The fallen king
scenes.say: Number five. The old champion that got knocked off its throne.

scenes.label: Fayum, Egypt
scenes.say: Meet Gigantophis. Its bones were found in the Fayum region of Egypt, from roughly forty million years ago.

scenes.label: The first giant
scenes.say: For a long time, it was the biggest snake anyone knew about. A true giant from the age after the dinosaurs.

scenes.label: A century of hype
scenes.say: It was named in 1901. And until Titanoboa came along in 2009, it was called the largest snake ever recorded. Some estimates said over ten meters.

scenes.label: 2017 re-check
scenes.say: But in 2017, two researchers in London took a fresh look at the bones. And they ran the numbers again, using its tail bones.

scenes.label: Guesses on guesses
scenes.say: Why redo it? Because back in 1901, the first estimate was about thirty feet. One bone can fool you.

scenes.label: About 6.9 m
scenes.say: Their estimate? About six point nine meters. Around twenty-three feet.

scenes.label: Beaten by a living snake
scenes.say: Here's the twist. That's huge. But it's actually shorter than a snake someone pulled out of the jungle in Indonesia just last winter.

scenes.label: Longest living snake
scenes.say: Which brings us to number four. The longest snake alive today.

scenes.label: Net pattern
scenes.say: The reticulated python. Named for the net-like pattern on its skin. It lives across Southeast Asia.

scenes.label: Sulawesi, Indonesia
scenes.say: In December 2025, news broke about a giant female on the island of Sulawesi, in Indonesia.

scenes.label: Meet the Baroness
scenes.say: She's called Ibu Baron. The Baroness. And in January 2026, a team finally measured her.

scenes.label: It took a crew
scenes.say: Several people had to lift her into place. Then they stretched a surveyor's tape from her head to the tip of her tail.

scenes.label: 7.22 m record
scenes.say: Seven point two two meters. That's twenty-three feet, eight inches. Guinness says she's the longest wild snake ever reliably measured.

scenes.label: Weighed like rice
scenes.say: And they weighed her in a canvas sack, on scales normally used for bags of rice. Ninety-six and a half kilos.

scenes.label: Hiding in plain sight
scenes.say: Think about that. A wild snake that long, and nobody had measured her until this year.

scenes.label: Maybe 7.9 m
scenes.say: And here's the crazy part. Snakes stretch out under anesthesia, and she wasn't put under. So her true length might be closer to seven point nine meters.

scenes.label: Wild pigs, buffalo
scenes.say: Pythons out there hunt things like wild pigs, and even anoa, a small wild buffalo. That's serious prey.

scenes.label: Medusa: 7.67 m
scenes.say: And she's not even the record in captivity. A python named Medusa, in Kansas City, measured seven point six seven meters back in 2011.

scenes.label: 7 to 8 m limit
scenes.say: So the longest living snakes top out around seven to eight meters. Remember that number. Because the next ones break it.

scenes.label: The heavyweight
scenes.say: Number three. The heaviest snake on Earth today.

scenes.label: Length vs bulk
scenes.say: The green anaconda. A python wins on length. But an anaconda wins on sheer bulk.

scenes.label: Up to 250 kg
scenes.say: The Smithsonian's National Zoo says they can reach up to two hundred fifty kilos. That's five hundred fifty pounds of muscle.

scenes.label: Eyes on top
scenes.say: Their eyes and nostrils sit on top of the head. So they can lie almost fully underwater, still watching, still breathing.

scenes.label: One meal, weeks
scenes.say: Adults eat deer, caimans, and capybaras. Then they might not eat again for weeks.

scenes.label: 20 to 40 babies
scenes.say: And the females are much bigger than the males. A mother gives birth to live babies in the water. Usually twenty to forty.

scenes.label: Record: 82
scenes.say: The biggest litter ever recorded? Eighty-two baby anacondas. At once.

scenes.label: Wait, two species?
scenes.say: But here's something most people missed. In 2024, scientists said the green anaconda is actually two species.

scenes.label: 5.5% different
scenes.say: The northern green anaconda differs from the southern one by about five and a half percent in its DNA. They split around ten million years ago.

scenes.label: Still hiding secrets
scenes.say: Some experts still argue about the name. But one thing is clear. The biggest snakes alive still hide secrets.

scenes.label: The new monster
scenes.say: Okay. Now we leave the living world. Number two is the snake that's in the news right now.

scenes.label: Kutch, India
scenes.say: In a lignite mine in Kutch, in western India, giant fossil bones turned up in the rock.

scenes.label: Not a crocodile
scenes.say: At first, researchers thought they belonged to an extinct crocodile. They were wrong.

scenes.label: 27 vertebrae
scenes.say: Scientists at IIT Roorkee studied twenty-seven vertebrae. The biggest one was over eleven centimeters wide.

scenes.label: King of serpents
scenes.say: They named it Vasuki indicus, after the king of serpents in Hindu mythology, the snake around Shiva's neck.

scenes.label: 11 to 15 m
scenes.say: It lived about forty-seven million years ago. And their estimate for its length? Somewhere between eleven and fifteen meters.

scenes.label: Up to 50 ft
scenes.say: At the top end, that's fifty feet. Picture two of the Baroness, nose to tail, and you're still short.

scenes.label: A lost family
scenes.say: It belonged to a lost family of snakes called madtsoiids. They lived across several continents, including India and Africa, for around a hundred million years.

scenes.label: About 28°C
scenes.say: Its world was warm, too. Researchers estimate around twenty-eight degrees Celsius. Remember that, because temperature comes back at the end.

scenes.label: Ambush hunter
scenes.say: How did it hunt? Probably slowly. Researchers think it lay in ambush and squeezed its prey, like anacondas do today. Something that big probably moved across land in slow, straight lines.

scenes.label: Big uncertainty
scenes.say: But here's the honest part. The scientists themselves say the estimate has a lot of uncertainty. Twenty-seven bones is not a whole snake.

scenes.label: Second biggest bones
scenes.say: So did Vasuki beat the champion? Nobody knows yet. Its vertebrae are the second biggest of any snake ever found. The biggest still belong to number one.

scenes.label: Titanoboa
scenes.say: Number one. The undisputed giant. Titanoboa.

scenes.label: Cerrejón, Colombia
scenes.say: Its fossils came out of the Cerrejón coal mine in Colombia. One of the biggest open-pit mines in the world.

scenes.label: Found in 2002
scenes.say: The first expedition went in 2002. A team from the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, with students from the University of Florida.

scenes.label: 186 fossils, 30 snakes
scenes.say: Scientists have found one hundred eighty-six fossils, from about thirty different snakes. So this wasn't a one-off freak.

scenes.label: After the dinosaurs
scenes.say: It lived around sixty million years ago. Just a few million years after the dinosaurs disappeared.

scenes.label: About 13 m
scenes.say: Length? About thirteen meters. Around forty-two feet.

scenes.label: 730 to 1,135 kg
scenes.say: Weight? The Smithsonian's team estimated over a ton. About eleven hundred kilos. One later study suggested closer to seven hundred thirty. Either way, that's several green anacondas in one snake.

scenes.label: The famous drawing
scenes.say: Now, you've probably seen drawings of Titanoboa crushing a crocodile. It's a great picture.

scenes.label: Mostly fish!
scenes.say: But here's the twist. Its skull suggests it mostly ate fish. The ultimate giant was, mostly, a fish eater.

scenes.label: Why not today?
scenes.say: So, the big question I promised at the start. Why is there no Titanoboa alive today?

scenes.label: Cold-blooded
scenes.say: Snakes are cold-blooded. Their bodies run on outside heat. And back then, the tropics were hot.

scenes.label: At least 32°C
scenes.say: From Titanoboa's size, Jason Head's team estimated the yearly average was at least thirty-two degrees Celsius. Hotter than today's rainforests.

scenes.label: A living thermometer
scenes.say: Jason Head put it simply. He said Titanoboa challenges our understanding of past climates. In other words, the snake was the thermometer.

scenes.label: Case closed?
scenes.say: So the simple answer is, the world cooled down, and giant snakes shrank. Case closed, right?

scenes.label: 183 fossil backbones
scenes.say: Not quite. In December 2025, a Cambridge team checked one hundred eighty-three fossil anaconda backbones from Venezuela.

scenes.label: Expected bigger
scenes.say: They were twelve million years old, from a warmer world. The team expected anacondas seven or eight meters long.

scenes.label: Same size as today
scenes.say: They found four to five meters. About the same as today. While giant caimans and turtles around them went extinct.

scenes.label: Heat is not everything
scenes.say: So heat helps. But it isn't the whole story. Other scientists think Titanoboa got huge because big mammals weren't competing with it yet. Some even argue that ancient rainforest wasn't much hotter than today's.

scenes.label: Still a mystery
scenes.say: Which means the real reason no Titanoboa exists today is still an open question. And somewhere, more bones are waiting in the ground.

scenes.label: Which one got you?
scenes.say: So which giant shocked you most? The Baroness, the eighty-two babies, Vasuki, or the fish-eating Titanoboa? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: The Biggest Snake Ever Ate… Fish?
short.description: Titanoboa was about 13 m long and weighed up to a ton, yet its skull suggests it mostly ate fish. Sources: Smithsonian (2009), Head et al., Nature.

scenes.say: The biggest snake ever found was about thirteen meters long.
Its bones came out of a giant coal mine in Colombia. One hundred eighty-six fossils, from about thirty snakes.
The longest snake alive today? A wild python measured this year at seven point two meters. Titanoboa was almost double.
And it may have weighed over a ton. It lived sixty million years ago, right after the dinosaurs.
You've seen drawings of it crushing crocodiles, right? Here's the twist. Its skull says it mostly ate fish.
Scientists think a hotter world let it grow that huge. But nobody knows for sure.
So next time someone tells you anacondas are huge, remember this. The biggest snake ever found
